children: The U.S. Supreme Court's justices appeared divided during oral arguments Monday, as the justices debated whether communities can sue big energy companies for billions of dollars to pay for local harms allegedly caused by climate-related damages that scientists say are tied to the worldwide burning of fossil fuels.

Justices across the ideological spectrum noted that state-backed lawsuits are routinely used to target other conduct with widespread effects, such as the manufacture of asbestos or the marketing of tobacco, although some expressed concern about opening the floodgates to cases against any company that contributed to greenhouse gas emissions,
The Wall Street Journal
reported.
The Supreme Court is weighing a lawsuit brought by Boulder County, Colorado, against Exxon Mobil
and Suncor Energy
claiming the companies deceived consumers about the dangers of their oil and gas operations and their effects on climate change through their advertising and marketing.

The Colorado Supreme Court allowed the suit to continue to state court, but the oil companies have asked the justices to overturn the ruling, arguing that Boulder's claims are pre-empted by the Clean Air Act.

"If Boulder's claims are allowed to go forward, some 90,000 municipalities across the country will have the ability to make national and international energy policy by asking juries to impose catastrophic damages on selected fossil fuel producers," Suncor's
attorney told the court.
But by the end of the day's arguments, only one member of the Supreme Court—Justice Kavanaugh—appeared squarely in the companies' camp, according to
WSJ
, saying prior Supreme Court cases have made clear that air and water pollution are exclusively federal, not state, issues.

Justice Alito, who owns stock in several energy companies, has recused himself, raising the possibility that the court could deadlock 4-4, which would leave in place the lower court decision that Boulder's lawsuit should proceed toward trial but without setting a nationwide precedent affecting other cases.
A decision is expected in the coming months.

Raymond James analyst Pavel Molchanov said the market was skeptical as it was unclear how much of the oil pledged under the new G7 agreement would come from the remaining volumes of the previously coordinated 400M-barrel emergency release announced in March by the International Energy Agency.

The U.S. Department of Energy said 800K barrels of crude were released from the Strategic Petroleum Reserve last week, leaving 283M barrels held in the reserve as of Friday, the lowest since October 1982.
Meanwhile, seven members of OPEC and its allies, including Saudi Arabia and Russia, agreed Sunday to keep production levels steady in November.
Saudi and Yemeni forces launched a counteroffensive to remove Houthi rebels from the strategic port city of Mokha to ease the threat to energy exports through the narrow Bab al-Mandeb Strait.
In response, the Houthis said they launched missile and drone attacks against multiple targets in Saudi Arabia, including King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh and an Aramco refinery in Rabigh.
